entries.title: 稳稳接住
entries.name: Performed Empathy
entries.request: 你正常说就行，别再说什么“稳稳接住我”了。
entries.quote: “你不是太敏感，你只是太清醒了。我就在这里，不躲、不藏、不绕，稳稳地接住你。”
entries.better: “我明白。把那段内容发来，我帮你看看哪里不对。”
entries.tagline: 把“我明白”说成“稳稳接住你”，意思能猜到，听起来却不像真人日常说话。
entries.why: “接住你、托住情绪”把普通回应换成了现实交流里很少出现的说法。每个词都没错，连起来却很别扭；模型反复这样说，就成了明显的 AI 口癖。
examples: 这一次，我会稳稳地接住你的每一份情绪。
你的疲惫，我先替你轻轻托住。
我会陪你把这一段情绪慢慢走完。
entries.normal: 小说、广告或角色台词本来就需要这种非日常表达。
entries.avoid: 先写真正想表达的意思，再看真人在当前场景里会不会这样说。普通回应直接说“我明白”“我来看看”就够了。
entries.prompt: 把“稳稳接住你、托住你的情绪”这类不自然的说法删掉。保留原意，改成真人在当前场景里会直接说的话。

entries.title: 单字动作
entries.name: Compressed Verbs
entries.request: 你怎么老说收一下、提一层、落回去？正常说话不这么说。
entries.quote: “先把问题收紧，把逻辑顺一下，再把结论往上提一层，最后稳稳落住。”
entries.better: “把第二段缩短，结尾直接写‘自动整理会议结论和待办’。”
entries.tagline: 一句话里反复用“提、收、落、顺”，像把普通说法硬改成一串单字动作。
entries.why: 这些字本来都是正常动词，AI 却喜欢把它们配给问题、逻辑、情绪和结论。“把情绪收一下、把力量提一层、最后稳稳落住”似懂非懂，真人很少这样密集地说。
examples: 这个点先接一下，再往下铺。
情绪往回收，力量再往上提。
前面铺开，后面拢住，最后往人身上落。
entries.normal: 剪辑、排版或表演指导中，这些动作有明确含义，而且团队平时就这样说。
entries.avoid: 先按日常说法重写。删掉“提、收、落、顺”以后原意没有变化，就不需要硬加这些动作。
entries.prompt: 删掉密集出现的“提、收、落、顺、接”这类单字动作。保留原意，改成真人在当前场景里会直接说的话。

entries.title: 什么都要加双引号
entries.name: Decorative Quotation Marks
entries.request: 这些词本来就是正常意思，为什么都要特意加个引号？
entries.quote: “我们先把‘真实’放回产品里，再让‘用户’重新成为体验的主角。”
entries.better: “先删掉没有来源的评价，再把真实用户反馈放到产品页。”
entries.tagline: 普通词也要加上双引号，好像每个词都另有深意。
entries.why: 双引号本来用于引用、特殊称谓或反讽。AI 却常给真实、用户、价值、看见、连接这类普通词加引号，硬造一种意味深长的语气，真人很少整段这样写。
examples: 让“价值”真正被“看见”。
把“人”重新放回“体验”中心。
这不是“功能”，而是一种“连接”。
entries.normal: 正在引用原话、标出特殊称谓，或上下文确实需要表示反讽。
entries.avoid: 删掉引号再读一遍。词义没有变化，就直接写这个词；只有真正的引用、特殊称谓和反讽才保留。
entries.prompt: 删掉普通词外面没有作用的双引号。只保留原话引用、特殊称谓和确实需要表达反讽的引号。

entries.title: 动不动就来个夸张比喻
entries.name: Inflated Metaphors
entries.request: 就说这个功能解决什么，别又写成灯塔、桥梁、钥匙。
entries.quote: “它不是一款普通工具，而是一座穿越信息迷雾的灯塔，为每一个迷失在效率洪流中的人照亮前路。”
entries.better: “它把散落的会议记录整理成结论和待办。”
entries.tagline: 普通功能被写成灯塔、桥梁、钥匙和引擎，句子很大，实际意思很小。
entries.why: 比喻本来是帮助人理解陌生关系。AI 却喜欢用灯塔、桥梁、钥匙、翅膀和引擎包装普通功能，有时一句话还混用好几个，读起来夸张又不自然。
examples: 为创作者插上想象的翅膀。
搭建人与信息之间的桥梁。
成为团队穿越不确定性的灯塔。
entries.normal: 一个统一的比喻确实能帮助读者理解复杂关系，而且全文没有继续混用其他比喻。
entries.avoid: 先写真实对象、动作和结果。比喻没有让关系更好懂，或者只是让句子显得宏大，就直接删掉。
entries.prompt: 删掉灯塔、桥梁、钥匙、翅膀、引擎这类夸张比喻。保留原意，直接写清对象、动作和结果。

entries.title: 提升立意
entries.name: Forced Elevation
entries.request: 这不就是个会议纪要功能吗？别一下扯到人与人连接那么大。
entries.quote: “它解决的从来不只是会议纪要的效率问题，更是在这个被技术加速的时代，帮我们重新找回人与人之间真实的连接。”
entries.better: “它把会议录音整理成结论和待办，减少会后手动整理。”
entries.tagline: 普通功能明明只解决一个小问题，却被写成人生、社会或时代意义。
entries.why: 文章可以有立意，但立意需要人物、冲突、长期影响或可验证的变化。没有材料时，拔高只会让结论大于事实。
examples: 一个待办清单，承载的是我们对生活秩序的重新想象。
这不仅是一次界面升级，更是对未来工作方式的温柔回应。
当技术退到身后，人终于可以重新成为时间的主人。
entries.normal: 原材料确实提供了长期影响、人物经历和足以支持判断的证据。
entries.avoid: 先写出材料和判断之间的关系；材料不足就停在产品实际解决的问题。
entries.prompt: 不要提升立意。结尾只保留原材料能够支持的结果，不增加时代、社会或人性意义。

entries.title: 满口砍一刀、收口、闭环
entries.name: Engineering Posture
entries.request: 你正常说就行，别一开口就是砍一刀、收口、闭环。
entries.quote: “这版我直接砍一刀：先把逻辑压实，再把结构收口，最后把方案落盘，形成一个最小闭环。”
entries.better: “我把重复的第二段删了，保存按钮也能用了。”
entries.tagline: 把普通修改说成“砍一刀、压实、收口、闭环”，像在硬套互联网黑话，听起来很不自然。
entries.why: 这些词并非不能用，做互联网和技术工作的人也会偶尔说。AI 的特点是把多个词密集地串在一句话里，不管当前场景是否需要，整段像在模仿某种职场口吻。
examples: 这里再补一刀，整体就更稳了。
先把逻辑压实，再把表达收口。
最后落盘，形成一个最小闭环。
entries.normal: 团队平时本来就这样说，而且单个词在当前工作里有明确含义。
entries.avoid: 保留真正必要的行业词，其余改成当前场景里最自然的说法，不要为了显得专业把几个黑话连在一起。
entries.prompt: 删掉“砍一刀、压实、收口、闭环、落盘”这类密集出现的互联网黑话。保留原意，改成真人在当前场景里会直接说的话。

entries.title: 动不动就夸你抓住本质
entries.name: User Validation
entries.request: 我只是问这个想法行不行，别又说我抓住了本质。
entries.quote: “你这个判断非常准确，而且已经触及了问题最本质、最关键的那一层。”
entries.better: “这个想法有一半成立：首屏确实太长，但主要问题是前两段重复，不只是字数多。”
entries.tagline: 不管你说什么，都用“非常准确、抓住本质、思考很深”来夸，像固定的捧场话。
entries.why: 真人会在有具体理由时肯定某一点，很少每次开口都先给一段高强度夸奖。AI 把它当成通用开场，语气会显得过度热情又不自然。
examples: 你这个判断非常精准。
你已经抓住最本质的那一层了。
这个思考非常深，也非常高级。
entries.normal: 对方确实做成了一件事，而且你能具体说出哪一点值得肯定。
entries.avoid: 需要肯定时只说具体哪一点；不需要时直接回应内容，不先套一段夸奖。
entries.prompt: 删掉“非常准确、抓住本质、思考很深”这类固定捧场话。直接回应我说的内容。

entries.title: 不是 X，而是 Y
entries.name: Forced Contrast
entries.request: 直接说这次更新做了什么，别又写成“不是更新，而是重新定义未来”。
entries.quote: “这不是一次简单的产品更新，而是一场关于效率、协作与未来工作方式的重新定义。”
entries.better: “这次更新把保存和发布拆成两个按钮，减少误发布。”
entries.tagline: 遇到什么都先写成“不是 X，而是 Y”，像给普通内容套上固定的反转句。
entries.why: 真人会在真正纠正误解时这样对比，AI 却把普通介绍也写成反转：不是工具，是伙伴；不是功能，是体验。句子看起来有力度，读多了却都像同一个模板。
examples: 不是功能，是体验。
不是工具，而是伙伴。
不只是效率，更是可能性。
entries.normal: 对方确实把 X 误解成 Y，需要用一句对比把两者分开。
entries.avoid: 没有真实误解要纠正，就直接说原本想表达的内容，不先制造一个反转。
entries.prompt: 删掉反复出现的“不是 X，而是 Y”“不只是 X，更是 Y”。保留原意，改成自然的直接陈述。

entries.title: 先说结论的套话
entries.name: Scripted Preamble
entries.request: 这个问题很简单，直接告诉我答案就行，不用先铺一大段。
entries.quote: “我先把结论放在前面：你的直觉完全正确。下面我用三点把这件事讲透。”
entries.better: “可以。这个属性只影响当前元素，不会改到其他卡片。”
entries.tagline: 答案还没出现，先来一句“直接说结论”，再宣布下面要分三点。
entries.why: 复杂回答可以先给结论，但普通问题每次都用“一句话总结、直接说结论、分三点讲透”，会让不同任务听起来像同一份脚本。
examples: 我先直接说结论：可以，而且非常值得。
一句话总结：方向完全正确。
先给答案，再把底层逻辑拆开讲清楚。
entries.normal: 内容很长，读者确实需要先知道结论，再决定是否继续阅读。
entries.avoid: 短问题直接回答。需要分点时，让分点来自内容，不先宣布自己要分几点。
entries.prompt: 直接回答问题，不要用“一句话总结、先说结论、下面分三点”作为固定开场。

entries.title: 每句话都拆成分点
entries.name: Fragmented List Writing
entries.request: 这几句话明明能顺着说完，为什么又拆成一堆圆点和编号？
entries.quote:
“结论：
• 能做
• 速度快
• 风险低
1. 先改
2. 再看
3. 最后确认”
entries.better: “可以做。先修改重复文案，再检查桌面和手机页面；确认显示与交互都正常后再提交。”
entries.tagline: 一个完整判断被拆成许多只有几个字的项目，读者还得自己把逻辑拼回去。
entries.why: 列表适合并列选项和操作步骤。AI 却常把连续说明切成标题、短横线、圆点和编号，每项只有几个字，因果、转折和条件都消失，阅读也变得不断起停。
examples:
— 背景：清楚
— 问题：较多
— 建议：优化

• 先梳理
• 再提升
• 最后完善

1. 可以
2. 推荐
3. 值得
entries.normal: 需要快速扫读一组并列项、检查清单，或必须按顺序完成的步骤。
entries.avoid: 因果、转折和条件用完整句子或段落说清。只有内容真正并列或有先后顺序时才用列表，并在每一项里写清对象和结果。
entries.prompt: 不要把连续说明拆成大量短分点，也不要混用短横线、圆点和编号。能用一两段完整句子说清就直接写；只有并列项或步骤才使用列表。

entries.title: 如果你愿意
entries.name: Automatic Follow-up
entries.request: 说完就行了，不用每次最后都问我要不要再来一版。
entries.quote: “如果你愿意，我下一步可以直接给你一版。”
entries.better: “三处重复句子已经删掉，标题和事实内容没有改。”
entries.tagline: 事情已经说完了，结尾还要问你要不要再来一版。
entries.why: 任务已经回答完时，固定邀约会拖长对话，还让结尾像客服脚本。
examples: 如果你愿意，我可以继续展开。
需要的话，我还能再给三个版本。
我也可以直接帮你落地。
entries.normal: 当前任务确实存在两个需要用户选择的分支。
entries.avoid: 任务完成就结束。只有缺少关键选择时，才提出一个具体问题。
entries.prompt: 完成当前任务后直接结束，不要自动邀请我继续下一步。

entries.title: Unlock / Elevate
entries.name: Abstract Boosters
entries.request: 这段话听着挺厉害，可我还是没看懂产品到底能干什么。
entries.quote: “Unlock your potential and elevate the experience.”
entries.better: “上传 CSV，得到图表和一段可编辑的结论。”
entries.tagline: 抽象动词承诺能力和提升，却不说明输入、输出和工作流程。
entries.why: 这些词本身没有错。多个抽象动作连续出现，而且用户仍不知道产品做什么时，文案就只剩气氛。
examples: Unleash creativity.
Empower every team.
Elevate your workflow.
entries.normal: 后面紧跟具体对象、操作和可验证结果。
entries.avoid: 写清用户提供什么，产品处理什么，最后得到什么。
entries.prompt: Replace abstract verbs with the actual input, action, and output.

entries.title: Delve
entries.name: Stock Analysis Verb
entries.request: 能不能直接说重点？别每次都从“Let’s delve into…”开始。
entries.quote: “Let’s delve into this fascinating topic.”
entries.better: “这次更新支持离线编辑，恢复网络后会自动同步改动。”
entries.tagline: 开头先宣布深入探讨，迟迟不说当前问题是什么。
entries.why: Delve 在正式写作里可以正常使用。它与 intricate、realm、journey 等抽象词成套出现时，更像生成模板。
examples: Delve into the intricacies.
Embark on a journey.
Explore the fascinating realm.
entries.normal: 文章确实需要正式语体，而且紧接着给出明确主题和分析对象。
entries.avoid: 从问题、对象或结论开始，不介绍自己即将如何写作。
entries.prompt: Start with the subject and conclusion. Do not announce that you will delve into it.

entries.title: Landscape / Tapestry
entries.name: Decorative Abstractions
entries.request: 这句到底想说什么？别绕什么 landscape、tapestry 了。
entries.quote: “Navigate the intricate tapestry of a changing landscape.”
entries.better: “产品会从客服工单中找出反复出现的问题。”
entries.tagline: 用风景、织物和旅程隐喻代替正在讨论的真实对象。
entries.why: 隐喻可以帮助理解；一段话连续堆叠多个隐喻时，读者反而更难确认主语和关系。
examples: the digital landscape
a rich tapestry of ideas
the ever-evolving ecosystem
entries.normal: 全文围绕同一个有解释作用的隐喻组织。
entries.avoid: 换回产品、用户、页面、数据和动作的真实名称。
entries.prompt: Use the real names of the product, user, data, and action instead of decorative metaphors.

entries.title: In Today’s World
entries.name: Universal Opening
entries.request: 前面这句时代背景可以删了，直接说现在到底变了什么。
entries.quote: “In today’s fast-paced, ever-evolving world…”
entries.better: “远程团队现在需要花更多时间检查异步更新。”
entries.tagline: 用任何主题都能套用的时代背景开头。
entries.why: 这类开头没有缩小问题，也没有提供信息。删除以后，正文通常可以直接开始。
examples: In the digital age…
In an ever-changing landscape…
Now more than ever…
entries.normal: 时代变化本身就是主题，而且后面有时间、事件或数据支撑。
entries.avoid: 第一句直接写当前变化、具体对象或读者需要处理的问题。
entries.prompt: Remove the universal opening and begin with the specific change or problem.

entries.title: 居中大标题
entries.name: Centered Hero Default
entries.request: 能不能先把产品界面放出来？现在又是一个大标题加两个按钮。
entries.quote: 大标题、两行说明、两个按钮永远居中排列。
entries.tagline: 不管产品是什么，都先放一个居中大标题、两行说明和两个按钮。
entries.why: 居中首屏适合单一、简短的主张。复杂产品仍套用同一结构时，真实界面和关键操作会被推到首屏以下。
examples: 标题占满首屏
两个同级按钮
产品界面只露出一角
entries.normal: 页面只需要传达一个简短主张，用户下一步也非常明确。
entries.avoid: 根据用户首先要判断的内容决定首屏：产品界面、数据、流程或操作都可以放在最前面。
entries.prompt: 先按用户进入页面后的主要任务安排 Hero，不要默认把标题和两个按钮全部居中。

entries.title: 三张等宽卡片
entries.name: Three-card Default
entries.request: 这三个功能明明有主次，为什么都做成一样大的卡片？
entries.quote: 所有功能都被压成三个同样大小、同样结构的卖点。
entries.tagline: 主要功能和次要功能全做成一样大的卡片，看不出先看什么、先做什么。
entries.why: 三张卡适合三个并列对象。主要功能、辅助功能和证据被做成同级时，用户看不出先后关系。
examples: 统一图标
统一标题长度
统一一行说明
entries.normal: 三个对象职责并列，信息量接近，用户不需要按顺序完成。
entries.avoid: 先标出主要任务和辅助信息，再按重要程度分配面积、位置和细节。
entries.prompt: 这三个功能重要程度不同，不要做成等宽卡片。按用户完成任务的顺序重新安排。

entries.title: 蓝紫渐变光球
entries.name: Purple Glow Default
entries.request: 怎么又是蓝紫渐变和发光球？这跟我们的品牌没什么关系。
entries.quote: 深色背景、蓝紫渐变、模糊光球和发光描边同时出现。
entries.tagline: 颜色和光效跟品牌、内容都没关系，只是为了看起来像“科技产品”。
entries.why: 紫色、渐变和光效都可以正常使用。它们与产品信息没有关系，而且整套出现时，页面很容易和其他生成站点相似。
examples: 模糊光球
发光边框
随机网格背景
entries.normal: 品牌本来使用这些颜色，或光效确实表示选中、运行和能量状态。
entries.avoid: 先使用品牌资产和真实界面；装饰效果需要能说明内容或状态。
entries.prompt: 保留有品牌依据的颜色，删除与内容和状态无关的渐变光球、发光边框和网格背景。

entries.title: 框里再套框
entries.name: Nested Containers
entries.request: 外面已经有一个框了，里面怎么又套了三层卡片？
entries.quote: 页面先装进大面板，区块再装进卡片，卡片里的标题、说明和按钮还各有一层边界。
entries.tagline: 页面已经有一个大框，里面的标题、说明和按钮又被一层层框起来。
entries.why: 边框本来是为了告诉用户“这是一个单独的东西”。AI 常把标题、说明和按钮全都装进框里，结果用户反而看不出哪些内容本来属于同一组。
examples: 卡片里面再套同样的卡片
标题和说明各有一层浅色框
整页已经有面板，列表项还重复描边
每个小标题都装进胶囊标签
entries.normal: 里面确实是一个可以单独查看或操作的东西，边框能帮助用户认出它。
entries.avoid: 先用标题、顺序和留白分组。只有内容确实独立，或者需要标出可以操作的范围时，才保留一层边框。
entries.prompt: 检查页面里一层套一层的框。删除没有实际作用的内层卡片，改用标题、顺序和留白分组。

entries.title: 每段都画分割线
entries.name: Divider Everywhere
entries.request: 这些内容本来就是一组，为什么每两行之间都要画一条线？
entries.quote: 标题下面一条线、说明下面一条线、每个列表项之间再一条线，页面被切成密密麻麻的小格。
entries.tagline: 内容本来连在一起，却到处画线，页面被切成一小块一小块。
entries.why: AI 容易把“分区清楚”直接理解成增加线条。线越多，用户越难判断哪些边界重要，连续内容也失去呼吸感。
examples: 每个标题下面都有横线
侧栏每个分类之间都加线
卡片已有描边，内部每行继续分隔
文章每两段之间插入一条线
entries.normal: 密集表格、菜单分组或相邻重复项确实需要边界帮助扫读。
entries.avoid: 先用间距和标题层级组织内容。只有相邻对象容易混淆时，才保留一条低对比度分割线。
entries.prompt: 删除页面里不表示真实分组变化的分割线。先用标题和间距分区，只在相邻内容仍难区分时保留浅色线。

entries.title: 左边都要加一条竖线
entries.name: Left-border Callout Default
entries.request: 这些都是普通说明，为什么每一块左边都要加一条彩色竖线？
entries.quote: 标题、说明和建议都被做成左侧带竖线的引用块，像每句话都需要重点强调。
entries.tagline: 普通内容也套上左侧竖线，引用、提醒和正文看起来没有区别。
entries.why: 左侧竖线常用来表示引用、提示、状态或选中。AI 容易把它当成通用装饰，给普通卡片和每段说明都加一根，甚至每块换一种颜色，结果边线抢走注意力，却没有稳定含义。
examples: 每张功能卡左侧都有一条彩色竖线
普通正文套用引用块样式
蓝、紫、绿竖线没有对应状态或分类
同一模块同时使用顶部强调线和左侧强调线
entries.normal: 内容确实是引用、告警或选中状态，而且左侧竖线在整套产品里始终表达同一含义。
entries.avoid: 普通内容先用标题、字号、留白和局部底色组织。只有竖线能稳定表示引用、状态或选择时才保留，并由同一个组件统一维护。
entries.prompt: 检查页面里所有左侧竖线。删除普通卡片和说明文字旁只用于装饰的边线；引用、告警或选中状态确实需要时，统一它的含义和样式。

entries.title: 又大又黑又挤
entries.name: Heavy Headline
entries.request: 这个标题又粗又挤，两行字都快贴在一起了，能不能先让它好读一点？
entries.quote: 长标题使用超大字号、最重字重和接近单倍的行高，换成两三行后挤成一块黑色。
entries.tagline: 标题同时又大、又粗、行距又小，换成两三行以后挤成一团。
entries.why: AI 常把“有冲击力”直接翻译成更大、更粗，却不检查中文笔画密度、长标题换行和手机宽度。
examples: 64px、900 字重配紧行高
长标题每一行都使用最重字重
页面标题和模块标题同样粗黑
手机换行后上下笔画几乎贴住
entries.normal: 标题很短，展示字体适合重字重，而且桌面和手机上的换行与可读性都已检查。
entries.avoid: 同时检查字号、字重、行高和标题长度。标题换行后先保证字面清楚，再决定需要多少视觉冲击。
entries.prompt: 重新检查这组标题的字号、字重和行高。降低黑块感，并在手机宽度下确认多行标题不拥挤。

entries.title: Emoji 当图标
entries.name: Emoji as Icons
entries.request: 这些火箭、星星、盾牌看着太模板了，换成正常一点的图标吧。
entries.quote: 每张功能卡都放一个大 Emoji：🚀 快速启动、✨ 智能生成、🛡️ 安全可靠。
entries.tagline: 不管功能是什么，都用火箭、星星、盾牌这类 Emoji 凑图标。
entries.why: Emoji 会随系统改变外观，大小、色彩和细节也难以统一。火箭、星星、盾牌被套进任何产品后，通常不能帮助用户区分真实功能。
examples: 🚀 极速体验
✨ AI 智能生成
🎯 精准触达
🛡️ 安全可靠
entries.normal: 品牌本来就使用 Emoji，或者页面面向儿童、聊天和轻松社交场景。
entries.avoid: 能通过标题理解时直接不用图标；确实需要识别时，选择同一套线性或填充图标，并让图形对应真实功能。
entries.prompt: 删除功能卡里的 Emoji。只有图标确实帮助识别功能时，才从现有图标库选择同一风格的图标。

entries.title: 每块都要飞进来
entries.name: Motion Everywhere
entries.request: 我只是往下看内容，为什么每一块都要晃一下才肯出现？
entries.quote: 标题淡入、卡片上浮、按钮弹跳、光点呼吸，滚动到哪里都要先等一段动画。
entries.tagline: 每个标题、卡片和按钮都在动，却没有帮助用户看懂页面发生了什么。
entries.why: 生成页面很容易把“加点微交互”执行成每个元素都动。单个效果看着精致，整页同时出现时会打断阅读，也可能让对动态敏感的用户不适。
examples: 每个区块滚动淡入
卡片悬停统一上浮
按钮和光点持续脉冲
entries.normal: 动效正在说明页面切换、对象来源、操作结果，或者品牌本身以动态叙事为核心。
entries.avoid: 先保留一次真正有解释作用的运动；其余内容直接显示，并支持系统的减少动态效果设置。
entries.prompt: 删除没有说明状态或空间关系的入场、上浮和脉冲动画。保留必要动效，并检查减少动态效果设置。

entries.title: 手机端一路堆到底
entries.name: Fake Responsive Layout
entries.request: 电脑版的侧栏、表格和按钮全挤成一条长页面，手机上反而更难用了。
entries.quote: 桌面三列全部改成单列，侧栏先出现，主任务被推到很下面，宽表格只能横着拖。
entries.tagline: 手机上只是把电脑版从上到下堆起来，重要内容反而更难找到。
entries.why: 响应式不是让布局“不溢出”就完成。小屏可用空间和操作方式都变了，仍照搬桌面顺序时，页面会更长，关键动作也更难找到。
examples: 侧栏排在正文前面
宽表格整体缩小
桌面工具栏挤成两三行
entries.normal: 内容本来就是同级列表，单列顺序与用户在手机上的任务顺序一致。
entries.avoid: 先保留手机上的主要任务，再折叠次要导航、改写表格呈现，并检查触控尺寸。
entries.prompt: 不要只把桌面布局改成单列。按手机上的主要任务重新安排导航、内容顺序、表格和操作按钮。

entries.title: 到处补说明
entries.name: Description Everywhere
entries.request: 这些分类名已经很清楚了，上面为什么还要再写一段“在这里管理你的知识”？
entries.quote: 工作区、分类、卡片、表单和按钮旁都补一段同义说明，页面上到处是“在这里……”和“帮助你……”。
entries.tagline: 说明只是把旁边的标题和按钮换个说法，没有增加任何新信息。
entries.why: AI 容易把“界面要清楚”理解成每个区域都要配一段解释。重复文案占用空间，也让真正会影响操作的信息更难被发现。
examples: 笔记侧栏在分类上方写“在这里管理你的知识”
“最近笔记”下面再写“查看你最近打开的笔记”
按钮“新建页面”旁补一句“点击这里创建新页面”
卡片标题“团队成员”下面写“管理你的团队成员”
表单标题“基本信息”下面写“请填写你的基本信息”
entries.normal: 说明补充了输入格式、适用条件、操作后果，或解释用户不熟悉的概念。
entries.avoid: 逐句检查：删掉以后信息没有减少，就直接删除。只保留会影响选择、输入和结果判断的说明。
entries.prompt: 删除侧栏、卡片和表单里只重复标题或按钮名称的说明。保留输入格式、条件、后果和陌生概念的必要解释。

entries.title: 同一操作换着叫
entries.name: Naming Drift
entries.request: 这里写“新建”，右上角又叫“添加”，打开弹窗以后怎么变成“创建”了？
entries.quote: 侧栏写“新建笔记”，空状态写“添加页面”，弹窗主按钮又写“创建文档”，其实都在完成同一个操作。
entries.tagline: 同一个对象和操作在不同位置换名字，用户无法确认它们是不是一件事。
entries.why: AI 会按局部语境补一个听起来合理的词，却没有维护整套界面的对象名称和动作名称。流程越长，名称越容易漂移。
examples: 新建、添加、创建指向同一个动作
保存、提交、完成指向同一个结果
删除、移除、清空没有说明后果差异
项目、空间、工作区其实是同一个对象
登录页叫账号，设置页又改称账户
entries.normal: 不同名称对应不同对象、范围或后果，而且界面能让用户看出差异。
entries.avoid: 为主要对象和动作确定一套名称，并在导航、按钮、弹窗、提示和错误信息中复用。
entries.prompt: 检查整个创建笔记流程。统一对象名和动作名，不要让“新建、添加、创建”指向同一个操作。

entries.title: 按钮只是摆设
entries.name: Inert Controls
entries.request: 这个筛选点了什么都不变，那为什么还要把它做得像真的一样？
entries.quote: 搜索、筛选、收藏和导出都有完整按钮外观，点击以后数据、状态和页面都没有变化。
entries.tagline: 按钮看起来能点，点完却没有任何变化，也没说明它还没做好。
entries.why: 生成工具擅长快速补齐界面外壳，容易把常见按钮一起画出来。用户会按外观理解它能用，点击无结果时只能猜是坏了、在加载，还是根本没做。
examples: 筛选后列表不变
收藏按钮没有选中状态
导出按钮只弹一个假成功提示
entries.normal: 页面已经明确写着“这里只是静态示意，暂时不能点”，用户不会把它当成做好的功能。
entries.avoid: 看起来能点就要有结果。暂不支持的按钮就删掉、置灰并说明原因，或写清楚这只是示意图。
entries.prompt: 逐个检查页面上看起来能点的按钮。让点击产生真实结果；暂不支持的操作就删除、置灰并说明原因。

entries.title: 只放图标，不写名字
entries.name: Icon Button Maze
entries.request: 这一排图标我根本不知道哪个是删除，手机上也没法悬停看提示。
entries.quote: 编辑、复制、分享、归档和删除都缩成相似的线性图标，没有文字名称。
entries.tagline: 编辑、分享、删除都只剩图标，用户只能靠猜。
entries.why: 图标能节省空间，但很多动作并没有人人都认识的图形。生成界面喜欢排一排图标显得简洁，却忘了写名称，也没有把删除这种危险操作单独说清。
examples: 表格每行五个无文字图标
只在悬停时显示作用
删除与归档使用相似符号
entries.normal: 图标人人都认识，用户也能看到它的名称，而且不会和旁边的操作混淆。
entries.avoid: 主要操作直接写名称；其他图标也要让用户看到名称，删除等危险操作还要单独确认。
entries.prompt: 检查所有图标按钮。主要操作直接显示文字，其他图标补上用户能看到的名称，并单独确认删除等危险操作。

catch-you.request: Skip the reassurance—I just need help finding what is wrong with this section.
catch-you.quote: “You are not too sensitive. You are simply clear-eyed. I am right here, and I will hold all of this with you.”
catch-you.better: “This section has two problems: the opening repeats itself, and the conclusion has no support. I’ll mark both sentences.”
catch-you.tagline: The response performs understanding and comfort before reviewing the facts.
catch-you.why: This language fits some counseling contexts. It sounds scripted when applied to slide edits, code review, or routine questions.
examples: This time, I truly understand.
You have carried this for too long. Leave the rest to me.
You do not need to explain. I will hold all of this for you.
catch-you.normal: The user has clearly expressed distress and the conversation calls for emotional support.
catch-you.avoid: Confirm the task first. Respond only to feelings the user has actually expressed.
catch-you.prompt: Confirm my task directly. Do not comfort me or interpret my emotions before reviewing the facts.

single-verbs.request: Just tell me which sentence to change. “Tighten it” and “land it” do not tell me much.
single-verbs.quote: “Tighten the problem, smooth the logic, raise the conclusion, then land it.”
single-verbs.better: “In paragraph two, replace ‘elevate collaboration’ with ‘turn meeting notes into decisions and assigned tasks.’”
single-verbs.tagline: Compressed action verbs omit the object, location, and expected result.
single-verbs.why: The sentence sounds active, but the reader cannot tell which paragraph, file, or interface state should change.
examples: Catch this point, then expand it.
Pull the emotion back and raise the force.
Open the first half, close the second, and land on the human point.
single-verbs.normal: A team shares the exact context and uses the phrase as live shorthand.
single-verbs.avoid: Name the object, editing location, and observable result.
single-verbs.prompt: Do not use compressed editing verbs. State the exact location and completed result.

raise-the-theme.request: It is just a meeting-notes feature. Why are we turning it into a statement about human connection?
raise-the-theme.quote: “It is not merely a faster way to write meeting notes. In an age accelerated by technology, it helps us rediscover genuine human connection.”
raise-the-theme.better: “It turns a meeting recording into decisions and action items, reducing manual follow-up.”
raise-the-theme.tagline: A routine feature receives social, personal, or historical meaning absent from the source.
raise-the-theme.why: A larger claim needs people, conflict, long-term impact, or evidence. Without them, the conclusion exceeds the facts.
examples: A to-do list carries our attempt to reimagine order in everyday life.
This is more than an interface update. It is a gentle answer to the future of work.
When technology steps back, people can finally become the owners of their time again.
raise-the-theme.normal: The source includes real people, long-term impact, and enough evidence for the claim.
raise-the-theme.avoid: Show the evidence behind the interpretation. Otherwise stop at the problem the product solves.
raise-the-theme.prompt: Do not inflate the theme. Keep the conclusion within the results supported by the source.

engineering-posture.request: Just tell me what changed. Phrases like “hard cut” and “close the loop” do not help.
engineering-posture.quote: “I made one hard cut: lock down the logic, close the structure, ship the plan, and form a minimum closed loop.”
engineering-posture.better: “I removed the repeated paragraph and connected Save to the existing submit flow. Save and refresh both pass.”
engineering-posture.tagline: A forceful engineering tone replaces the actual change, evidence, and verification.
engineering-posture.why: Engineering metaphors can be valid. Applied to every task, they communicate posture without telling the reader what changed.
examples: Add one more cut.
Build the minimum closed loop.
This approach is harder and more robust.
engineering-posture.normal: The team is discussing a real engineering boundary and the object is already explicit.
engineering-posture.avoid: Report what was removed, added, preserved, and tested.
engineering-posture.prompt: Replace engineering posture with exact files, fields, states, and test results.

user-validation.request: Please stop telling me I am right. I just want to know whether this idea actually works.
user-validation.quote: “Your judgment is exactly right, and it reaches the deepest and most essential layer of the issue.”
user-validation.better: “Your idea is partly right: the hero is too long, but the main problem is repeated content, not word count alone.”
user-validation.tagline: The response certifies the user as correct or insightful before checking the premise.
user-validation.why: Unsupported praise can hide a false premise. The user needs a judgment and evidence, not validation.
examples: That is an exceptionally elegant conclusion.
Your thinking is already remarkably deep.
You are already an expert in this field.
user-validation.normal: The response names the specific claim and provides evidence that supports it.
user-validation.avoid: State which facts hold and which assumptions need correction.
user-validation.prompt: Do not rate my insight. Check my premise and explain the conclusion with evidence.

not-x-but-y.request: It is just a product update. Why does it sound like we are redefining the future?
not-x-but-y.quote: “This is not a simple product update. It is a redefinition of efficiency, collaboration, and the future of work.”
not-x-but-y.better: “This update separates Save from Publish, reducing accidental publishing.”
not-x-but-y.tagline: A fixed contrast creates the appearance of insight without a useful distinction.
not-x-but-y.why: Contrast helps when two concepts are genuinely easy to confuse. Repetition turns every small change into a grand claim.
examples: Not a feature, but an experience.
Not a tool, but a partner.
Not only efficiency, but possibility.
not-x-but-y.normal: X and Y are easy to confuse and the text explains their boundary.
not-x-but-y.avoid: Remove the frame and read the remaining claim. If no information is lost, keep the direct sentence.
not-x-but-y.prompt: Remove the “not X, but Y” frame and state what the feature changes.

conclusion-first.request: This is a simple question. Can you just give me the answer without the long setup?
conclusion-first.quote: “Let me put the conclusion first: your instinct is completely right. I will unpack it in three points.”
conclusion-first.better: “Yes. This property affects only the current element, not the other cards.”
conclusion-first.tagline: A fixed preamble announces the conclusion, structure, and authority before answering.
conclusion-first.why: Long answers may need a summary. Repeating “one-line answer,” “bottom line,” and “three points” across routine questions makes every task sound scripted.
examples: The short answer: yes, and it is absolutely worth doing.
In one sentence: your direction is completely right.
First the answer, then I will unpack the underlying logic.
conclusion-first.normal: The material is long and readers need the conclusion before deciding whether to continue.
conclusion-first.avoid: Answer short questions directly. Let sections emerge from the content instead of announcing a fixed count.
conclusion-first.prompt: Answer directly. Do not use “the short answer,” “bottom line,” or “three points” as a standard opening.

fragmented-bullets.request: These ideas belong in a sentence. Why split them into a pile of bullets and numbered fragments?
fragmented-bullets.quote:
“Conclusion:
• Feasible
• Fast
• Low risk
1. Revise
2. Review
3. Confirm”
fragmented-bullets.better: “This is feasible. Revise the repeated copy, then check the desktop and mobile pages. Submit only after the layout and interactions work.”
fragmented-bullets.tagline: One connected judgment becomes a stack of tiny fragments, leaving the reader to reconstruct the logic.
fragmented-bullets.why: Lists help with peer options and ordered steps. Generated answers often split continuous reasoning into headings, dashes, bullets, and numbers so that causes, conditions, and contrasts disappear.
examples:
— Context: clear
— Problems: several
— Advice: improve

• Review
• Enhance
• Polish

1. Feasible
2. Recommended
3. Worthwhile
fragmented-bullets.normal: Readers need to scan peer items, a checklist, or steps that must happen in a specific order.
fragmented-bullets.avoid: Use sentences and paragraphs for causes, conditions, and contrasts. Use a list only for real peers or sequence, and name the object and result in each item.
fragmented-bullets.prompt: Do not split continuous reasoning into many short bullets or mix dashes, bullets, and numbers. Use complete sentences unless the content is a true list or sequence.

if-you-want.request: That answers it. You do not need to offer another version every time.
if-you-want.quote: “If you want, I can immediately produce another version.”
if-you-want.better: “I removed the three repeated sentences. The heading and factual content are unchanged.”
if-you-want.tagline: Every answer ends by selling another round of work.
if-you-want.why: When the task is complete, an automatic invitation lengthens the exchange and makes the ending feel scripted.
examples: I can keep expanding if you want.
I can also provide three more versions.
I can help you implement it next.
if-you-want.normal: The task has two real branches and requires a user choice.
if-you-want.avoid: End when the task is complete. Ask one concrete question only when a decision is missing.
if-you-want.prompt: Finish the current task and stop. Do not automatically invite another step.

abstract-boosters.request: This sounds impressive, but I still cannot tell what the product actually does.
abstract-boosters.quote: “Unlock your potential and elevate the experience.”
abstract-boosters.better: “Upload a CSV and get a chart plus an editable written summary.”
abstract-boosters.tagline: Abstract verbs promise improvement without naming an input, output, or workflow.
abstract-boosters.why: The words can be valid. A cluster of them becomes filler when the reader still cannot tell what the product does.
examples: Unleash creativity.
Empower every team.
Elevate your workflow.
abstract-boosters.normal: A concrete object, action, and verifiable outcome follow immediately.
abstract-boosters.avoid: Name what the user provides, what the product does, and what it returns.
abstract-boosters.prompt: Replace abstract verbs with the actual input, action, and output.

delve.request: Can you just get to the point instead of opening with “Let’s delve into…”?
delve.better: “This release adds offline editing and syncs changes when the connection returns.”
delve.tagline: The opening announces analysis before naming the current problem.
delve.why: Delve is normal in formal writing. It becomes a tell when bundled with abstract words such as intricate, realm, and journey.
examples: Delve into the intricacies.
Embark on a journey.
Explore the fascinating realm.
delve.normal: The piece needs a formal register and immediately names a clear subject.
delve.avoid: Begin with the problem, object, or conclusion.
delve.prompt: Start with the subject and conclusion. Do not announce that you will delve into it.

landscape-tapestry.request: What does this actually mean? Please drop the landscape and tapestry metaphors.
landscape-tapestry.quote: “Navigate the intricate tapestry of a changing landscape.”
landscape-tapestry.better: “The product finds repeated issues across support tickets.”
landscape-tapestry.tagline: Scenery and textile metaphors replace the real object being discussed.
landscape-tapestry.why: A metaphor can clarify one relationship. Several metaphors in one sentence make the subject harder to identify.
examples: the digital landscape
a rich tapestry of ideas
the ever-evolving ecosystem
landscape-tapestry.normal: The whole piece uses one metaphor that materially improves understanding.
landscape-tapestry.avoid: Use the real names of the product, user, data, and action.
landscape-tapestry.prompt: Replace decorative metaphors with the real product, user, data, and action.

in-todays-world.request: Skip the broad opening and tell me what has actually changed.
in-todays-world.better: “Remote teams now spend more time reviewing asynchronous updates.”
in-todays-world.tagline: A universal era-setting opening can be attached to almost any subject.
in-todays-world.why: It does not narrow the problem or add information. The next sentence can usually begin the piece.
examples: In the digital age…
In an ever-changing landscape…
Now more than ever…
in-todays-world.normal: Historical change is the subject and the text provides dates, events, or data.
in-todays-world.avoid: Open with the specific change, object, or problem.
in-todays-world.prompt: Remove the universal opening and begin with the specific change or problem.

centered-hero.request: Can we show the product first? Right now it is just another big headline with two buttons.
centered-hero.quote: A large heading, two lines of copy, and two buttons are always centered.
centered-hero.tagline: The hero ignores the product task, available evidence, and primary action.
centered-hero.why: A centered hero works for one short claim. Complex products need room for the interface or evidence users must judge first.
examples: Oversized heading
Two equal buttons
Product UI pushed below the fold
centered-hero.normal: The page has one short claim and one obvious next step.
centered-hero.avoid: Choose the hero around the first thing users need to judge: interface, data, process, or action.
centered-hero.prompt: Arrange the hero around the user’s main task. Do not center a heading and two buttons by default.

three-equal-cards.request: These three things are not equally important. Why do they all get the same card?
three-equal-cards.quote: Every feature becomes one of three equal cards.
three-equal-cards.tagline: A neat three-column layout hides real differences in priority and sequence.
three-equal-cards.why: Three cards work for three peer objects. They fail when a primary task, supporting feature, and evidence become equal.
examples: Matching icons
Matching title length
Matching one-line descriptions
three-equal-cards.normal: The three objects are peers and do not require an order.
three-equal-cards.avoid: Rank the main task and supporting information before assigning space and position.
three-equal-cards.prompt: These features have different priorities. Do not present them as three equal cards.

purple-glow.request: Why is everything glowing purple? It does not look like our brand.
purple-glow.quote: Dark background, purple gradient, blurred orb, and glowing border appear together.
purple-glow.tagline: Visual effects create generic “tech” atmosphere without a brand or state-related reason.
purple-glow.why: Purple and gradients can be valid. The full bundle becomes generic when it has no relationship to product information.
examples: Blurred orb
Glowing border
Decorative grid background
purple-glow.normal: The brand uses these colors or the glow communicates a real selected or running state.
purple-glow.avoid: Start with brand assets and product UI. Keep decoration only when it explains content or state.
purple-glow.prompt: Keep brand-backed color and remove gradients, glows, and grids that explain no content or state.

rounded-everything.request: The outer panel already has a boundary. Why are there three more cards inside it?
rounded-everything.quote: The page sits in a panel, each section sits in a card, and the card’s heading, copy, and actions get more containers.
rounded-everything.tagline: Containers replace content relationships, so more boundaries make the page feel fragmented.
rounded-everything.why: A container can identify an independent object or interaction area. Generated interfaces often package every heading, description, and action without deciding which content belongs together.
examples: Cards nested inside matching cards
Separate boxes around a heading and its description
Outlined list items inside an outlined panel
A pill above every small heading
rounded-everything.normal: The component is independent or interactive and the boundary helps identify it.
rounded-everything.avoid: Group with headings, order, and whitespace first. Keep one boundary only for an independent object, interaction area, or state.
rounded-everything.prompt: Audit nested containers. Remove inner cards that do not mark an independent object or interaction area, then group with headings, order, and whitespace.

divider-everywhere.request: These items already belong together. Why is there a rule between every two lines?
divider-everywhere.quote: There is a rule below the heading, another below the description, and more between every item until the page becomes a grid.
divider-everywhere.tagline: Rules appear without real boundaries, replacing whitespace, headings, and content order.
divider-everywhere.why: Generated interfaces often translate “clear sections” directly into more lines. When every boundary is visible, users cannot tell which one matters and continuous content loses breathing room.
examples: A rule below every heading
Dividers between every sidebar item
A bordered card with more rules between every row
A horizontal rule between every two paragraphs
divider-everywhere.normal: Dense tables, grouped menus, or adjacent repeated items need a boundary to support scanning.
divider-everywhere.avoid: Use spacing and heading hierarchy first. Keep one subtle divider only when adjacent objects remain hard to distinguish.
divider-everywhere.prompt: Remove dividers that do not mark a real group change. Organize with headings and spacing first, then keep a subtle rule only where adjacent content is still unclear.

left-border-callouts.request: These are ordinary descriptions. Why does every block need a colored line on the left?
left-border-callouts.quote: Headings, descriptions, and advice all become quote-like blocks with a colored left border, as if every sentence were a callout.
left-border-callouts.tagline: Ordinary content gets a left accent border until quotes, alerts, and body copy look the same.
left-border-callouts.why: A left border can identify a quote, notice, state, or selection. Generated interfaces often reuse it as decoration on ordinary cards and paragraphs, sometimes with a different color on every block and no stable meaning.
examples: A colored left border on every feature card
Ordinary body copy styled as a blockquote
Blue, purple, and green borders with no state or category meaning
A top accent and left accent on the same section
left-border-callouts.normal: The content is a real quote, alert, or selected state, and the left border carries the same meaning throughout the product.
left-border-callouts.avoid: Organize ordinary content with headings, type, spacing, and restrained backgrounds. Keep the border only when it consistently communicates a quote, state, or selection.
left-border-callouts.prompt: Audit every left accent border. Remove decorative borders from ordinary cards and descriptions; keep one consistent treatment only for real quotes, alerts, or selected states.

heavy-headline.request: This heading is huge, heavy, and cramped. Can we make the two lines readable first?
heavy-headline.quote: A long heading uses an oversized font, the heaviest weight, and near-solid line height until two or three lines form a dark block.
heavy-headline.tagline: Size, weight, and tight line height become strong at the same time, turning a multiline heading into a dark block.
heavy-headline.why: Generated designs often translate “impactful” into bigger and heavier type without checking long titles, dense glyphs, or mobile wrapping.
examples: 64px type at weight 900 with tight leading
Every line of a long title uses the heaviest weight
Page and section headings carry equal weight
Mobile wrapping leaves almost no space between lines
heavy-headline.normal: The heading is short, the display face supports heavy weight, and wrapping and readability have been checked on desktop and mobile.
heavy-headline.avoid: Check size, weight, line height, and copy length together. Preserve legibility after wrapping before adding visual impact.
heavy-headline.prompt: Review heading size, weight, and line height together. Reduce the dark-block effect and verify multiline headings at mobile width.

emoji-icons.request: Can we lose the rockets and sparkles? They make the feature cards look generic.
emoji-icons.quote: Every feature card gets a large emoji: 🚀 Fast launch, ✨ AI generation, 🛡️ Enterprise security.
emoji-icons.tagline: Generic emoji replace a deliberate icon system and add a colorful symbol to every heading.
emoji-icons.why: Emoji change across operating systems and are hard to align in size, color, and detail. Rockets, sparkles, and shields rarely distinguish the product’s actual features.
examples: 🚀 Lightning fast
✨ AI-powered
🎯 Precision targeting
🛡️ Secure
emoji-icons.normal: Emoji are part of the brand, or the product serves children, chat, or casual social use.
emoji-icons.avoid: Remove the icon when the title is enough. When recognition needs an icon, use one consistent set and match each symbol to the real feature.
emoji-icons.prompt: Remove emoji from the feature cards. Use the existing icon library only when an icon helps identify the feature.

motion-everywhere.request: I am just reading the page. Why does every section have to move before it appears?
motion-everywhere.quote: Headings fade in, cards rise, buttons bounce, and glowing dots pulse as every scroll position triggers another animation.
motion-everywhere.tagline: Motion explains no state or spatial relationship; it only delays and moves the content.
motion-everywhere.why: A request for micro-interactions can easily become movement on every element. Each effect looks polished alone, but together they interrupt reading and can make motion-sensitive users uncomfortable.
examples: Every section fades in on scroll
Every card lifts on hover
Buttons and glows pulse forever
motion-everywhere.normal: Motion explains a page transition, object origin, or action result, or dynamic storytelling is central to the brand.
motion-everywhere.avoid: Keep one movement that actually explains something. Show the rest immediately and honor reduced-motion preferences.
motion-everywhere.prompt: Remove entrance, lift, and pulse animations that explain no state or spatial relationship. Keep necessary motion and test reduced-motion preferences.

fake-responsive.request: The sidebar, table, and buttons are all squeezed into one long mobile page. It is harder to use than desktop.
fake-responsive.quote: Three desktop columns become one stack, the sidebar comes first, the primary task moves far down, and the wide table still scrolls sideways.
fake-responsive.tagline: Mobile only stacks desktop content instead of reconsidering tasks, navigation, and touch controls.
fake-responsive.why: Responsive design is not finished when overflow disappears. The available space and input method change on a small screen; copying desktop order creates a longer page and hides the primary action.
examples: Sidebar before the main content
A wide table scaled down
Desktop toolbar wrapped onto three lines
fake-responsive.normal: The content is a true peer list and its single-column order matches the mobile task.
fake-responsive.avoid: Keep the primary mobile task first, collapse secondary navigation, adapt tables, and verify touch targets.
fake-responsive.prompt: Do not merely stack the desktop layout. Reorder navigation, content, tables, and actions around the primary mobile task.

description-everywhere.request: These category names are already clear. Why add “Manage your knowledge here” above them?
description-everywhere.quote: Workspaces, categories, cards, forms, and buttons all get a paraphrased description full of “here you can” and “helps you.”
description-everywhere.tagline: Supporting copy adds no condition, format, or consequence; it only repeats the nearby label or action.
description-everywhere.why: Generated interfaces often interpret “make it clear” as “explain every region.” Repeated copy takes space and makes information that actually affects an action harder to find.
examples: A notes sidebar says “Manage your knowledge here” above its categories
Recent notes is followed by “View notes you opened recently”
New page is followed by “Click here to create a new page”
Team members is followed by “Manage your team members”
Basic information is followed by “Enter your basic information”
description-everywhere.normal: The copy provides a format, condition, consequence, or an explanation of an unfamiliar concept.
description-everywhere.avoid: Delete a sentence if removing it loses no information. Keep only copy that changes a choice, input, or interpretation of the result.
description-everywhere.prompt: Remove sidebar, card, and form descriptions that only repeat headings or actions. Keep necessary formats, conditions, consequences, and unfamiliar concepts.

naming-drift.request: This says New, the empty state says Add, and the dialog says Create. Are they the same action?
naming-drift.quote: The sidebar says New note, the empty state says Add page, and the dialog button says Create document even though all three start the same action.
naming-drift.tagline: The same object or action changes names across the interface, so users cannot tell whether it is still the same thing.
naming-drift.why: A generated interface can choose a locally plausible word for each screen without maintaining shared product nouns and verbs. Longer flows drift more easily.
examples: New, add, and create mean one action
Save, submit, and finish mean one result
Delete, remove, and clear have unexplained consequences
Project, space, and workspace name one object
Sign-in uses account while settings uses profile for the same object
naming-drift.normal: Different terms identify different objects, scopes, or consequences, and the interface makes that difference clear.
naming-drift.avoid: Choose one noun and verb for each primary object and action, then reuse them in navigation, buttons, dialogs, messages, and errors.
naming-drift.prompt: Audit the full note-creation flow. Use one object name and one action name instead of switching between New, Add, and Create.

inert-controls.request: Nothing changes when I click this filter. Why make it look functional?
inert-controls.quote: Search, filter, favorite, and export all look complete, but clicking changes no data, state, or page.
inert-controls.tagline: A high-fidelity shell looks finished while its controls have no real result or prototype boundary.
inert-controls.why: Generation tools can complete a familiar interface shell quickly and add common controls by default. Users read those controls as functional and cannot tell whether silence means broken, loading, or never implemented.
examples: Filtering leaves the list unchanged
Favorite has no selected state
Export only shows a fake success toast
inert-controls.normal: A wireframe or demo clearly states that it is static and participants know the interaction is out of scope.
inert-controls.avoid: Every visible control needs a real result and feedback. Remove, disable with an explanation, or mark unsupported actions as static.
inert-controls.prompt: Audit every control that looks clickable. Implement a real result and feedback, or remove the interactive appearance when the action is unsupported.

icon-button-maze.request: I cannot tell which icon deletes the item, and there is no hover hint on a phone.
icon-button-maze.quote: Edit, copy, share, archive, and delete are reduced to similar line icons with no visible names.
icon-button-maze.tagline: Critical actions become pictures users must guess, while touch and assistive technology receive no name.
icon-button-maze.why: Icons can save space, but many actions have no stable universal symbol. Generated interfaces often use a clean row of icons while omitting visible labels, accessible names, and confirmation for dangerous actions.
examples: Five unlabeled icons on every table row
Meaning appears only on hover
Archive and delete use similar symbols
icon-button-maze.normal: The symbol is highly conventional, has an accessible name, and the context prevents ambiguity.
icon-button-maze.avoid: Name primary actions directly. Give secondary icons visible help and accessible names, and never make dangerous actions a guessing game.
icon-button-maze.prompt: Audit every icon button. Show text for primary actions, add visible help and accessible names elsewhere, and confirm destructive actions.

zh.title: 防止 AI 味儿
zh.description: 把常见的 AI 口癖、套模板的页面和不好用的交互当成词条来认。每条都给出原句或原页面、正常用法和具体改法。
zh.boundary: 单个词、视觉元素或交互问题不能证明作者。判断时要看它是否与其他默认选择成组出现。
zh.why: 为什么看起来像 AI 默认
zh.prompt: 可以这样告诉 AI Agent
zh.writingVisual: 用户指出以后，回答应该怎么变
zh.interfaceVisual: 同一个任务，改前和改后有什么区别

en.title: Avoid AI Slop
en.description: Browse recurring writing tells, UI defaults, and UX shortcuts like glossary entries. Each entry includes examples, valid uses, and a concrete revision rule.
en.boundary: One word, visual choice, or interaction bug cannot prove authorship. Judge repeated defaults in context.
en.writingVisual: How the answer should change after the user objects
en.interfaceVisual: What changes when the same task is designed deliberately
